diabetes.e: From Latin diabētēs (“siphon”), from Ancient Greek διαβήτης (diabḗtēs), from Ancient Greek διαβαίνω (diabaínō, “to pass through”).

s.d: a polygenic disease characterized by abnormally high glucose levels in the blood; any of several metabolic disorders marked by excessive urination and persistent thirst

(uncountable) Diabetes mellitus; any of a group of metabolic diseases whereby a person (or other animal) has high blood sugar due to an inability to produce, or inability to metabolize, sufficient quantities of the hormone insulin.
(humorous, slang, uncountable) Any food or beverage with a high amount of sugar.

diabetes insipidus.e: Learned borrowing from Latin diabetes insipidus (“tasteless diabetes”), as opposed to diabetes mellitus (“sweet diabetes”) because of the absence of glucose in urine in the former.

diabetes mellitus.e: Learned borrowing from New Latin diabetes mellitus (“diabetes of the sweet type”) (from the fact that in centuries past, physicians sometimes tasted a patient's urine to help diagnose the illness).

s.d: diabetes caused by a relative or absolute deficiency of insulin and characterized by polyuria
x: when doctors say ‘diabetes’ they usually mean ‘diabetes mellitus’

s.d: (uncountable) A medical disorder commonly called diabetes, characterized by varying or persistent hyperglycemia (high blood sugar levels), especially after eating. It is classified in two types, which are different etiologically but similar in clinical effects: type 1 and type 2.

s.d: To vanish.
To go missing; to become a missing person.
x: Eighteen years after Jaycee Dugard disappeared in 1991, she was found alive in the summer of 2009.

s.d: To go away; to become lost.
x: A turban and loincloth soaked in blood had been found; also a staff. These properties were known to have belonged to a toddy drawer. He had disappeared.

s.d: (euphemistic) To make vanish; especially, to abduct or murder for political reasons.
x: The Chinese government is well-known for disappearing particularly vocal political dissidents.

 "I don’t know."
 "What will you do if they decide to disappear you?"

gradually ceasing to be visible
ceasing to exist

s.d: (uncountable) The action of disappearing or vanishing.
x: Wireless phone technology led to the disappearance of once-common coiled cords for telephone handsets.

As hundreds of volunteers and police scoured parks and waterways in an area of New Orleans Tuesday, there were many questions but few answers about the disappearance 11 days ago of a 26-year-old teacher.

the act of leaving secretly or without explanation

x: Sudden and extensive disappearings and fresh appearings would startle and confound us, and if continued, would shatter our sense of personality out of us.

disappoint.e: From Middle English disapointen, disapoynten, from Middle French desapointer, desappointer (modern French désappointer). The word originally meant “to dispossess of an office”, and eventually broadened to mean “to frustrate the expectations or desires of” and “to defeat the realization or fulfillment of”. Modern nonstandard use of the original sense 6 is by analogy with appoint. By surface analysis, dis- + appoint.

s.d: fail to meet the hopes or expectations of
x: Her boyfriend let her down when he did not propose marriage

s.d: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.
x: His lack of respect disappointed her.
I was disappointed by last year’s revenue.

s.d: To deprive (someone of something expected or hoped for).
x: They that haue money in their purse, are afrayde and in doubte, yea and are continuallye martyred with feare, leaste GOD should disappoint them of their pray, and abate their portion.
[…] you shan’t be disappointed of a wedding—you shall come to mine.

s.d: (dated) To fail to meet (an expectation); to fail to fulfil (a hope).
x: […] his life was despaired of; and all Japan was filled with alarm and apprehension at the prospect of an infant’s ascending the throne: […] Their fears, however, were happily disappointed by the recovery of the emperor,
“But perhaps your accommodations—your cottage—your furniture—have disappointed your expectations?”

s.d: (dated) To show (an opinion, belief, etc.) to be mistaken.
x: I am sure you will not disappoint my opinion of you, by failing at any time to treat your aunt Norris with the respect and attention that are due to her.
“Well, I thought it was too good to be true,” he said at last, with a sigh of disappointed conviction.

s.d: (obsolete) To prevent (something planned or attempted).
x: He [God] disappointeth the devices of the crafty, so that their hands cannot perform their enterprise.

The wary Trojan shrinks, and bending low
Beneath his Buckler, disappoints the Blow.

s.d: (obsolete, rare) To dispossess (someone) of an office.
x: [W]e may comprehend [regal rights] vnder eight ſoueraigne marks: namely, […] to appoint or to diſappoint the greateſt officers: […]
[V]ersus the earlier one[s] who become hereditary sheriffs, the new ones were appointed and disappointed at the whim of the King.

dissect.e: Borrowed from Latin dissectus past participle of dissecare (“to cut asunder, cut up”), from dis- (“asunder”) + secare (“to cut”); see section.

s.d: cut open or cut apart

s.d: make a mathematical, chemical, or grammatical analysis of; break down into components or essential features
x: analyze a specimen
analyze a sentence

s.d: To study an animal's anatomy by cutting it apart; to perform a necropsy or an autopsy.
x: She was the first person in her class to properly dissect the sheep heart.

s.d: To study a plant's or other organism's anatomy similarly.
(figuratively) To analyze an idea in detail by delineating between its parts.

(derogatory, figuratively) To decontextualize an idea, especially through overanalysis by delineating between its parts too strongly based on style, usually involving pedantry, at the expense of substance.
x: Academics tend to take Indigenous oral histories out of their contexts and dissect them according to Western disciplinary objectives and foci (see figure 1).
By focusing excessively on dissecting the text into 'forms' and exploring their supposed evolution, form criticism overlooks the larger literary and historical context within which these forms exist.

s.d: To separate muscles, organs, etc. without cutting into them or disrupting their architecture.
x: Now dissect the triceps away from its attachment on the humerus.

s.d: Of an infection or foreign material, following the fascia separating muscles or other organs.
having one or more indentations reaching nearly to the midrib
Deeply divided; cut into many segments.

dissection.e: Borrowed from Latin dissectiōnem, perhaps via Middle French dissection. By surface analysis, dissect + -ion.

s.d: cutting so as to separate into pieces
a minute and critical analysis
detailed critical analysis or examination one part at a time (as of a literary work)
(uncountable) The act of dissecting.
(uncountable) Something dissected.
(figuratively, uncountable) A minute and detailed examination or analysis.
(uncountable) Surgical removal.
x: neck dissection
lymph node dissection

dissemble.e: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. Doublet of dissimulate, dissimilate, and dissimule. Displaced native Old English mīþan.

s.d: make believe with the intent to deceive
x: He feigned that he was ill
He shammed a headache

s.d: hide under a false appearance
x: He masked his disappointment

s.d: behave unnaturally or affectedly
x: She's just acting

s.d: To disguise or conceal something.
x: Dissemble all your griefs and discontents.
Perhaps it was right to dissemble your love.

s.d: To feign, dissimulate.
x: And like a Lyon, Slumbring in the vvay, / Or Sleep-diſſembling, vvhile he vvaits his Prey, […]
He soon dissembled a sleep.

s.d: To deliberately ignore something; to pretend not to notice.
To falsely hide one's opinions or feelings.
x: VVhile to his Arms the bluſhing Bride he took; / To ſeeming Sadneſs ſhe compoſ'd her Look; / As if by Force ſubjected to his VVill, / Tho' pleaſ'd, diſſembling, and a VVoman ſtill.

dissembler.e: A modification of earlier dissimuler (from Middle English dissimulour) after resemble and semblance; equivalent to dissemble + -er.

s.d: a person who professes beliefs and opinions that he or she does not hold in order to conceal his or her real feelings or motives
Someone who dissembles.
x: [T]he Earl vvas the vvorſe Philoſopher, being a great Reſenter and a vveak Diſſembler of the leaſt diſgrace: […]

s.d: pretending with intention to deceive
the act of deceiving
(uncountable) The action of the verb dissemble
x: The lies and dissemblings about this period are beyond most people's imaginations.

spreading by diffusion
Tending to disseminate, or to become disseminated (scattered, or widespread), spreadable.

One who, or that which, disseminates.

dissension.e: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

s.d: disagreement among those expected to cooperate
a conflict of people's opinions or actions or characters

(uncountable) Strong disagreement; a contention or quarrel; discord.
x: […]wherby at the last shuld have sourded discention amonge the people, they beinge seperately enclined towarde theyr naturall souerayne lorde[…]
In Biblical times the resort to chance was an agreed-upon way of making many decisions because it ended dissension among opposing, often powerful, parties.

dissent.e: From Middle English dissenten, from Latin dissentiō, dissentīre (“to differ in sentiments, disagree, be at odds, contradict, quarrel”), from dis- + sentiō, sentīre (see sense).

s.d: (law) the difference of one judge's opinion from that of the majority
x: he expressed his dissent in a contrary opinion

s.d: a difference of opinion
the act of protesting; a public (often organized) manifestation of dissent
(uncountable) Disagreement with the ideas, doctrines, decrees, etc. of a political party, government or religion.
x: ethnopolitical dissent
A system that suppresses dissent is fault-intolerant, ignorant and fragile.

s.d: (uncountable) An act of disagreeing with, or deviating from, the views and opinions of those holding authority.
(uncountable) A separate opinion filed in a case by judges who disagree with the outcome of the majority of the court in that case
(uncountable) A violation that arises when disagreement with an official call is expressed in an inappropriate manner such as foul language, rude gestures, or failure to comply.
x: City had been woeful, their anger at their own inertia summed up when Samir Nasri received a booking for dissent, and they did not have a shot on target until the 66th minute.

s.d: withhold assent
x: Several Republicans dissented

s.d: express opposition through action or words
x: dissent to the laws of the country

s.d: be of different opinions
x: I beg to differ!
She disagrees with her husband on many questions

s.d: To disagree; to withhold assent. Construed with from (or, formerly, to).
x: Where a trustee refuses either to assent or dissent, the Court will itself exercise his authority.
Those who openly dissented from the acts which the King had carried through the Parliament.

s.d: To differ from, especially in opinion, beliefs, etc.
x: Some are so eristical and teasty, that they will not ... bear with any that dissent.

Natural reason dictates, that motion ought to be assigned to the bodies, which in kind and essence most agree with those bodies which do undoubtedly move, and rest to those which most dissent from them.

s.d: (obsolete) To be different; to have contrary characteristics.
x: it was wholly unlawful, in any thing to dissent from him

s.d: talk at length and formally about a topic
x: The speaker dissertated about the social politics in 18th century England

s.d: To make a dissertation; to discourse.

s.d: To write one's dissertation.
x: Mark stayed up until 2 a.m. dissertating last night.

s.d: a treatise advancing a new point of view resulting from research; usually a requirement for an advanced academic degree

write up a dissertation

s.d: A lengthy lecture on a subject; a treatise; a discourse; a sermon.

s.d: To disserve, to provide a disservice to; to provide harmful or inadequate service to.

s.d: To separate (two or more things); to split apart (something).

A person who formally opposes the current political structure, the political group in power, the policies of the political group in power, or current laws.
x: I once more find myself a dissident, and a dissident in a very small minority.

Other prominent Chinese dissidents and activists on the platform reported a plunge in follower counts, too. The panic also spread to YouTube, an important source of income for many exiled dissidents, including Li.

s.d: A member of a paramilitary that has continued actions after the Good Friday Agreement or other ceasefire.
One who disagrees or dissents; one who separates from the established religion.

(historical) One who disagrees or dissents; one who separates from the established religion.: Sometimes Dissident: in the kingdom of Poland, the name for Christians not part of the Roman Catholic Church.
x: A Socinian was a Dissident, and a member of the Greek Church was a Dissident; and these Dissidents agreed to act together. Even a liberal Romanist might be called a Dissident.
The rest, about half a million Russian Orthodox and about the same number of Protestants, were known as ‘dissidents’; the huge Jewish community defied classification.

s.d: characterized by departure from accepted beliefs or standards
disagreeing, especially with a majority

On flattening either the higher or lower reed separately, by partially pushing in either one of the pulls, dissident beats instantly arose, which would be made to disappear by partially pushing in the other reed.

s.d: Continuing violent actions despite a ceasefire (especially the Good Friday Agreement).

s.d: the emergence of seeds as seed pods burst open when they are ripe

We may, however, notice Impàtiens, merely for the purpose of alluding to the dissilient property of its capsules, which, when ripe, burst with such force as to scatter the seeds to a considerable distance around.

s.d: hide (feelings) from other people
To practise deception by concealment or omission, or by feigning a false appearance; to dissemble.
To disguise or hide by adopting a false appearance; to dissemble.
x: [P]ublic feeling required the meagreness of nature to be dissimulated by tall barricades of frizzed curls and bows.

s.d: (rare) To connive at; to wink at; to pretend not to notice.

s.d: (obsolete) Feigned, simulated, pretended, false.
x:
Where they may win ought : by fayre diſimilate ſhow,
There they flickar, and flatter, in fauer to grow.

s.d: the act of deceiving
(uncountable) The act of concealing the truth; hypocrisy or deception.
x: Perhaps it was best to tell Ethel at once: if ever she went into society at all, she would inevitably hear of it, and her own concealment would have the appearance of a dissimulation,—the furthest from her thoughts.

s.d: (uncountable) Hiding one's feelings or intentions.
concealing under a false appearance with the intent to deceive
x: dissimulative arts

s.d: Of or pertaining to dissimulation.
x: The dissimulative phase of pathocracy

s.d: a person who professes beliefs and opinions that he or she does not hold in order to conceal his or her real feelings or motives
One who dissimulates.

dissipate.e: The verb is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the adjective from 1606 to 1765; from Middle English dissipaten, from Latin dissipātus, perfect passive participle of dissipō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), also written dissupō (“to scatter, disperse, demolish, destroy, squander, dissipate”), from dis- (“apart”) + supō (“to throw”). Doublet of dissipe (“to dissipate”), now obsolete.

s.d: to cause to separate and go in different directions
x: She waved her hand and scattered the crowds

s.d: move away from each other
x: The crowds dispersed

s.d: spend frivolously and unwisely
x: Fritter away one's inheritance

s.d: live a life of pleasure, especially with respect to alcoholic consumption
To drive away, disperse.
x:
August 1773, James Cook, journal entry

The extreme tendency of civilization is to dissipate all intellectual energy.

s.d: To use up or waste; squander.
x: The vast wealth […] was in three years dissipated.

s.d: To vanish by dispersion.
To cause energy to be lost through its conversion to heat.
x: The traction motors serve as generators when dynamic braking is used, the generated output being dissipated in fan-cooled resistance banks mounted in a removable roof section.

s.d: (colloquial, dated) To be dissolute in conduct.
(obsolete) dissipated
unrestrained by convention or morality

deplorably dissipated and degraded

s.d: preoccupied with the pursuit of pleasure and especially games of chance
x: led a dissipated life
a betting man

s.d: Wasteful of health or possessions in the pursuit of pleasure.

s.d: (uncountable) The act of dissipating or dispersing; a state of dispersion or separation; dispersion; waste.

18th century, Patrick Henry in a parliamentary debate
to reclaim the spendthrift from his dissipation and extravagance
I rose by candle-light, and consumed, in the intensest application, the hours which every other individual of our party wasted in enervating slumbers, from the hesternal dissipation or debauch.

dizen.e: From dialectal dize (“to put tow on a distaff”), from Middle English *disen, from Old English *disan, *disian, from *dise, *disen (“bunch of flax on a distaff”), from Proto-Germanic *disanō (“distaff”), of unknown origin, equivalent to dize + -en. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Diezene (“bundle of flax, distaff”), Middle Low German dise, disene (“distaff”).

s.d: dress up garishly and tastelessly
To dress with flax for spinning.
To dress with clothes; attire; deck; bedizen.
x: Like a tragedy queen he has dizen'd her out, / Or rather like tragedy giving a rout.

s.d: (UK, dialectal) To dress showily; adorn; dress out.
x: I tell you, these Englishwomen have either no life at all in them, or they're nothing but animal life. 'Gad, how they dizen themselves! They've no other use for their fingers. The wealth of this country's frightful!'

dizzy.e:
From Middle English dysy, desy, dusi, from Old English dysiġ (“stupid, foolish”), from Proto-West Germanic *dusīg (“stunned; dazed”).
Akin to West Frisian dize (“fog”), Dutch deusig, duizig (“dizzy”), duizelig (“dizzy”), German dösig (“sleepy; stupid”).

s.d: To make (someone or something) dizzy; to bewilder.
x: Let me have this violence and compulsion removed, there is nothing that, in my seeming, doth more bastardise and dizzie a wel-borne and gentle nature […]
If the jangling of thy bells had not dizzied thy understanding.

s.d: Producing giddiness.
